description: We are Team Cosmic Web, a team of four with a combined skill set spanning QA, UX design, coding, and 3D art. Together, we bring educational insight, creativity, and technical expertise to build experiences that make learning engaging and accessible.
summary: Crophalo is a free farm web app that answers the Field Shift challenge: which crop rotation will make this field stronger and more resilient? A farmer finds a field on the map, draws its outline, and answers four short questions about crops, water, soil and priorities. Crophalo then reads that exact place's own record, from NASA POWER weather since 2001 to NASA satellite pictures of plant greenness, soil moisture, rain, land temperature and groundwater, and compares three crop-rotation strategies side by side: what the farmer grows now, our suggestion, and another option worth a look. Each strategy shows why it was suggested, the evidence behind it, the benefits it may offer, where information is missing, and the risks to check locally. A hard-year test plays all three strategies on a hard year taken from this land's real weather, and a Change and see panel lets the farmer change water, tillage, soil or priorities and watch the plans move. Fields can be kept in My farm and viewed in 3D with NASA map layers. Scores come from fixed, readable rules, so every number can be explained and traced to its source. Crophalo speaks plain words, needs no account, keeps data on the farmer's own device, and is open source under Apache 2.0. Every screen is drawn from our own design system.
details:
WHY WE BUILT IT

Farmers face shifting temperatures, changing rain, water shortages and tired soils, and the choice of the next crop is made with very little evidence from their own field. Crophalo is a decision-support tool for exactly this choice. It brings NASA Earth observations, local crop knowledge and the farmer's own priorities into one clear place, and it helps the farmer explore rotation strategies that could strengthen soil health and adapt the farm to changing conditions. It supports the farmer's judgment and local expertise; it never replaces them.

WHAT WE ACCOMPLISHED

During this challenge we built a complete, working, open-source product, not a mock-up. It is live on the web at crophalo.earth, and a farmer can go from an empty screen to a compared, explained crop-rotation plan for a real field in a few minutes. Specifically, we (1) turned NASA Earth observations into plain answers for one field; (2) built a rule-based engine that scores rotations from the field's own weather record and compares three strategies, each with why it was suggested, the evidence, the benefits, where information is missing and the risks; (3) built a cloud-free map the farmer draws on, with eleven NASA and terrain layers; (4) built My farm, with a map board and a 3D view of every field; (5) designed and built our own design system, so every screen looks and behaves the same; and (6) documented every data source with its licence and citation.

HOW WE HELP FARMERS

- Better decisions with evidence: the farmer sees how each rotation would behave on their own land's weather record, instead of guessing or relying on a regional average.

- Time saved: a compared plan in minutes, free, with no account to create.

- Water and soil in view: strategies are scored against what matters to the farmer, such as saving water and building soil health, so options that protect soil and conserve water become visible.

- Resilience: the hard-year test shows how each strategy copes when a bad year comes.

- Trust: every number shows its source and date, and scores come from readable rules, so a farmer or an adviser can see why a strategy ranks where it does.

- Respect for local knowledge: the farmer states priorities and limits (equipment, workers, markets, crops they will not grow), can change any answer and watch the plans move, and every strategy lists what to check locally.

- Access: plain words, read-aloud buttons, US or metric units, a layout that works on a phone, private by design, and offline after one visit.

WHAT THE FARMER DOES

1. Find the field: search a place, use the device location, or open a demo field (near Mead, Nebraska, or near Beltsville, Maryland). Draw the field as a rectangle or by its corners on a cloud-free satellite map, or draw it with the keyboard. 2. Your crops: choose what grows there now. For fields in the United States and Canada, Crophalo reads the national crop maps (USDA Cropland Data Layer and Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada) and shows what the field grew year by year, with one press to use that rotation. 3. Water and soil: rain-fed or irrigated, how the field is worked, and what the soil is like. 4. What matters most: water saving, soil health, steady income, feed for animals, less fertiliser to buy, and limits such as no small-seed drill, few workers or machines, and crops the farmer will not grow.

THE ANSWER: THREE STRATEGIES, ALWAYS COMPARED

The report opens on "What should I plant next?" and then compares at least three strategies, always including the rotation the farmer has now: what you grow now, our suggestion, and another option worth a look. For every strategy Crophalo shows why it was suggested, what evidence supports it, what benefits it may offer, where information is missing, and which risks need a local check. Each strategy has a score with a plain-words fit label and a one-line description of what changes from today's rotation. "Your hardest year" takes a hard year from the land's own weather record and plays all three strategies on it, month by month, so the farmer sees where each one would be hurt. "Change and see" lets the farmer change how the field gets water, how it is worked, the soil and what matters most, and watch the three plans change at once. The report can be printed or saved as a PDF to share with an adviser, and Add to My farm keeps the field and its plan.

NASA DATA AT WORK

NASA POWER supplies the daily temperature, rain and ground wetness record of every field since 2001, and the scores are worked out from it together with the crops' water and warmth needs, the autumn frost date and the sowing and harvest windows. NASA SMAP soil moisture, GPM IMERG rain, GRACE and GRACE-FO water storage, ECOSTRESS ground temperature, Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2 greenness, MODIS vegetation and NASA FIRMS fires are read for the field's own place. Eleven map layers show how the land behaves: NASA GIBS plant greenness, soil moisture, rain rate and land temperature with legends and dates; NASA FIRMS fires; regional water storage from GRACE-FO; and slope, erosion exposure, frost pockets, sun and shade, and relief worked out from height tiles built partly from NASA SRTM. Satellite records and ground records are labelled separately, and every figure carries its date and source behind an "i" button. Scientific terms are explained in plain words.

SEE THE FIELD

My farm keeps several farms and fields. Each field has a map board and a 3D view of one field, one plan and one date, lit by one sun, showing what covers the ground through the year, with layers for slope, erosion exposure, frost pockets, greenness and shade. The home screen is a turning Earth with the 13 real satellites whose data Crophalo reads, on their real orbits; a press on a satellite opens its card, and choosing a place starts a short fall from orbit down to the field.

OUR OWN DESIGN SYSTEM

We did not use an off-the-shelf template. We designed and built Crophalo's own design system: one set of design tokens (colour, type, corners, shadows, spacing, sizes and motion, kept in a single tokens file) and one shared stylesheet that draws every control, card, list, loading skeleton, sheet and the logo in the app. A living page of the system is public at https://crophalo.earth/design.html, and it is drawn by the app's own stylesheet, so it cannot drift from the product. Every screen follows written UI rules: touch targets of at least 44 pixels, a clearly marked chosen state (blue fill, white bold words), skeleton loaders while data loads, calm motion that can be reduced, and layouts checked at 320 pixels wide with the largest text. The result is one calm, consistent tool from the first screen to the 3D view.

BUILT FOR PEOPLE

No account and no sign-in. Fields and plans stay on the farmer's own device, with a backup file. After one visit the app opens offline. Read-aloud buttons, keyboard drawing on the map, large touch targets, US or metric units, motion that can be reduced, and plain-language text throughout. Every source is listed on the Data page with its licence and citation.

HOW IT IS BUILT

Plain JavaScript with no framework, so it stays light; Leaflet for the map; three.js for the 3D view; a small Node.js server; and Python to read NASA satellite files from NASA Earthdata. Scores come from fixed, written rules with their sources (FAO crop water and ecology guides, university extension guides and the national crop maps), not from a black box, so any number can be explained. The code is open source under the Apache 2.0 licence.

IMPACT AND CREATIVITY

Any farmer with a phone or a computer can compare rotations for a real field in a few minutes, free, with NASA evidence instead of guesswork, and advisers can use the printed report as the start of a conversation. The creative parts are the fall from the Earth to the field with real satellites, the hard-year test of all three strategies on the land's own weather, Change and see, and a 3D field that shows what covers the ground.

USE OF SI TOOLS

Our team chose what to build, directed the work, and reviewed and tested the result. SI coding tools helped write Crophalo's code (including the icons and drawings made in code), its tests and its documents, and the narration of the 30-second video is a synthetic voice, which the video says. Crophalo itself does not use SI or machine learning to work out its answers; it uses fixed rules and counts over the public data named above.
dataRefs: NASA POWER daily weather and climate record (since 2001)
NASA SMAP L4 root-zone soil moisture (SPL4SMGP)
NASA GRACE and GRACE-FO water storage (JPL mascons)
NASA and USGS Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2 (HLS) surface reflectance
NASA MODIS vegetation index and land temperature
NASA FIRMS fires and hot spots
NASA GIBS satellite images (map layers and the Blue Marble satellite base)
NASA SRTM and NASADEM elevation (behind the height tiles)
projectRefs: USGS The National Map aerial photographs (satellite map close to the ground)
EOX Sentinel-2 cloudless 2016 (Copernicus Sentinel-2 pictures, CC BY 4.0)
Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada Annual Crop Inventory
USDA NRCS Soil Survey (SSURGO) through Soil Data Access
Open-Meteo forecast and ERA5 weather record (Copernicus Climate Change Service, ECMWF)
FAO-56 crop water guide (Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56)
Terrain Tiles land heights (Tilezen, AWS Open Data)
Environment and Climate Change Canada weather stations
USDA Agricultural Marketing Service Market News
National Corn Handbook NCH-40 (Purdue University Extension)
